paras: The attempted lynching of a street dentist's patient in New Orleans was a mob attack on an unnamed Black man that took place on or before December 1888, after a rumor spread that he was killing a white boy. Police stopped the mob before he was beaten to death, and the case reached the northern press as an ironic example of how 'the race issue' filled southern papers.

According to a New Orleans paper, an itinerant dentist working at a street corner had persuaded an 'immense colored man' to have two teeth drawn. As the dentist pulled, a 'mischievous boy' stuck a pin into the patient, who seized the boy and, in the paraphrase's words, inflicted 'a well-merited punishment.'

A rumor then went through the crowd that 'a colored man was murdering a white boy,' and a mob tried to seize the man. The mob gave him a 'bad scalp wound,' but he escaped to the second story of a nearby house. When a policeman tried to take him into custody there, he jumped to the ground, where the mob caught him. The account says the mob would have beaten him to death but for the interference of the police, while the boy's injuries were pronounced 'slight.'
No report of arrests, charges against the man or members of the mob, or any later proceedings appears in the coverage, and neither the man, the boy nor the officers are named.

The only surviving version is a paragraph in the exchange column of the Vermont Watchman of Montpelier on December 26, 1888, credited to a paper called the 'Transcript,' which had in turn summarized an unnamed New Orleans paper. The paragraph opened with the remark that 'the race issue certainly is the means of enlivening the local columns of southern papers' and framed the episode as the 'serious results' of a practical joke. Its wording was openly sardonic, crediting the mob with 'pleasant anticipations of lynching him' and noting the 'great solicitude' shown for a boy whose injuries were slight.
No copy of the original New Orleans report, with its date and its own framing, appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of a street dentist's patient in New Orleans
bases: A mob, said to have had 'pleasant anticipations of lynching him,' tried to seize a Black man, wounded him in the scalp and caught him, and would have beaten him to death but for the police; no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching (A1).

A mob acting without authority on a rumor that a Black man was 'murdering a white boy' attacked him, but police stopped it before he was killed, so it was an attempt, not a lynching under the standard definition (A1).
The only report is a secondhand paraphrase in one Vermont paper, credited to a 'Transcript' that took it from an unnamed New Orleans paper (A1).

accounts.label: New Orleans paper, as paraphrased by the 'Transcript' and the Vermont Watchman
accounts.gist: A boy's prank with a pin led the patient to punish him; a rumor that a colored man was murdering a white boy brought a mob that wounded and chased the man until police intervened.

framing.detail: Introduced with 'The race issue certainly is the means of enlivening the local columns of southern papers,' the item ironically called the mob's aim 'pleasant anticipations of lynching' and noted the 'great solicitude' for a boy with 'slight' injuries.

sources.note: Exchange-column paragraph, credited '—Transcript.', paraphrasing an unnamed, undated New Orleans paper: a boy stuck a pin into a 'colored' patient of a street dentist, the man punished the boy, and a mob on the rumor that he was murdering a white boy wounded and chased him until police intervened.
quotes: a mischievous boy stuck a pin into the patient. The patient became impatient, and, seizing the tormenting boy, inflicted upon him a well-merited punishment.
Immediately the rumor went out through the crowd that a colored man was murdering a white boy, and the mob, with pleasant anticipations of lynching him, attempted to seize the negro.
The mob caught him, and would have beaten him to death but for the interference of the police.
The race issue certainly is the means of enlivening the local columns of southern papers.
